Read Data

weekly_expense <- read.csv("weeklyexpence.csv")
glimpse(weekly_expense)
Rows: 40
Columns: 6
$ Name                        <chr> "Radha", "Prerana", "Chris", "Nireeksha", …
$ Gender                      <chr> "Female", "Female", "Male", "Female", "Mal…
$ Total_Expenditure_Last_Week <dbl> 2000.0, 1200.0, 15000.0, 3620.0, 560.0, 22…
$ X                           <lgl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA…
$ X.1                         <lgl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA…
$ X.2                         <lgl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA…
weekly_expense <- weekly_expense %>%
  mutate(
    Name = str_squish(Name),
    Gender = str_squish(Gender)
  )

gender_summary <- weekly_expense %>%
  group_by(Gender) %>%
  summarise(
    Average_Expenditure = mean(Total_Expenditure_Last_Week, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_Expenditure = sum(Total_Expenditure_Last_Week, na.rm = TRUE),
    Count = n()
  )

gender_summary

Hypothesis

  • Null Hypothesis: There is no difference between the true mean weekly expenditure for Male and Female.

  • Alternative Hypothesis: There is a significant difference between the mean weekly expenditure for Male and Female.

Visualising data

weekly_expense %>%
  gf_dhistogram(
    ~Total_Expenditure_Last_Week,
    fill = ~Gender,
    alpha = 0.5,
    title = "Weekly Expenditure by Gender"
  ) %>%
  gf_facet_grid(~Gender) %>%
  gf_fitdistr(dist = "dnorm") %>%
  gf_refine(scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2")) %>%
  gf_theme(theme(legend.position = "none"))
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.

Inference

  • Most girls spend a small amount of money, and their spending is very consistent.

  • The spending habits of boys are much more spread out and less consistent than the spending of girls.

  • The highest individual spenders in the dataset are all boys.

weekly_expense %>%
  gf_boxplot(
    Total_Expenditure_Last_Week ~ Gender, orientation = "x" ,
    fill = ~Gender
  ) %>%
  gf_refine(scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2"))

Inference

  • A few boys who spent a lot of money (outliers) made the average spending for all boys look much higher than it really is for most of them.
weekly_expense %>%
  gf_jitter(
    Total_Expenditure_Last_Week ~ Gender,
    color = ~Gender,
    alpha = 0.6,
    title = "Individual Weekly Expenditures"
  )
weekly_expense %>%
  group_by(Gender) %>%
  summarise(Average_Spend = mean(Total_Expenditure_Last_Week, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  gf_col(
    Gender ~ Average_Spend,
    fill = ~Gender,
    title = "Average Weekly Expenditure by Gender"
  ) %>%
  gf_refine(scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2"))
weekly_expense %>%
  gf_violin(
    Total_Expenditure_Last_Week ~ Gender,
    fill = ~Gender,
    alpha = 0.7,
    title = "Distribution of Weekly Expenditure by Gender"
  ) %>%
  gf_refine(scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2"))
obs_diff_expense <- diffmean(
  Total_Expenditure_Last_Week ~ Gender,
  data = weekly_expense,
  only.2 = FALSE
)
obs_diff_expense
diffmean 
4502.745
  • This is difference is huge because the male expense is not evenly distributed and because of few outliers the mean difference is high.
shapiro.test(weekly_expense$Total_Expenditure_Last_Week[weekly_expense$Gender == "Female"])

    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

shapiro.test(weekly_expense$Total_Expenditure_Last_Week[weekly_expense$Gender == "Male"])

    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  weekly_expense$Total_Expenditure_Last_Week[weekly_expense$Gender == "Male"]
W = 0.56351, p-value = 1.261e-06

Inference

  • The weekly expenditure data for both males and females is not normally distributed. This is also strongly supported by histogram chart.
var.test(
  Total_Expenditure_Last_Week ~ Gender,
  data = weekly_expense
)

    F test to compare two variances

Inference

  • There is a statistically significant difference in the variability (spread) of the weekly expenditures between males and females.

  • This also we saw in the graphs that Male spending is far more spread out and inconsistent than Female spending on the histogram chart.

Inference

  • The p-value (0.056) is slightly above the level 0.05. T the observed difference in average weekly expenditure between males and females is not statistically significant.

Conclusion

  • Boys Spend More! Overall, boys spend a higher amount of money than girls do.

  • Boys Spending is Messy (t-Test): Boys’ spending habits are very unpredictable (some spend very little, a few spend huge amounts), but girls’ spending is much more consistent.

  • Outliers Confuse Tests: A few boys who spent giant amounts (the outliers) made the standard average tests (like the t-test) unreliable and unable to clearly prove the difference.

  • Mann-whitney test that ignores those extreme high amounts, it confirms that the difference in spending between the genders is real with difference 1100 Rs.
